claim_verdicts.evidence: refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt 9.3.4: "The PUT method requests that the state of the target resource be created or replaced with the state defined by the representation enclosed in the request message content." / "If the target resource does not have a current representation and the PUT successfully creates one, then the origin server MUST inform the user agent by sending a 201 (Created) response." / if it does have one and it is modified, "the origin server MUST send either a 200 (OK) or a 204 (No Content) response". 9.2.2: "PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent."

Not in the local mirror: refs/rfc holds 6265/9110/9111/9112 only, and grep "PATCH" rfc9110.txt returns just three hits, none defining it ("[RFC5789] Dusseault, L. and J. Snell, 'PATCH Method for HTTP'"). WebFetch of rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5789 Section 2 returned verbatim: "With PATCH, however, the enclosed entity contains a set of instructions describing how a resource currently residing on the origin server should be modified"; "PATCH is neither safe nor idempotent"; "A PATCH request can be issued in such a way as to be idempotent".

refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt 9.3.5: "If a DELETE method is successfully applied, the origin server SHOULD send" ... "a 204 (No Content) status code if the action has been enacted and no further information is to be supplied, or" ... "a 200 (OK) status code if the action has been enacted and the response message includes a representation describing the status" (202 listed first), so the hedged "typically 204" holds. 9.2.2: "PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent"; "the request will have the same intended effect ... though the response might differ".

Enumerated every .cs file at the tag (git -C examples/don-hang ls-tree -r --name-only stage-1 | grep '\.cs$', then git show stage-1:<file> | grep 'HttpPut\|HttpDelete'): zero matches across the whole tree. OrdersController.cs at stage-1 declares only [HttpPost] (Create), [HttpGet("{id:int}")] (Get) and [HttpPatch("{id:int}/cancel")] (Cancel). So PATCH /api/v1/orders/{id}/cancel is indeed the only non-POST write endpoint, and section 5's "This API has no real `PUT` or `DELETE` endpoint at this stage" holds.

claim_verdicts.evidence: refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt 9.3.5: "content received in a DELETE request has no generally defined semantics, cannot alter the meaning or target of the request" and "A client SHOULD NOT generate content in a DELETE request unless it is made directly to an origin server that has previously indicated, in or out of band, that such a request has a purpose and will be adequately supported." That is a SHOULD NOT with an explicit exception, which is exactly what section 4's "normally carries no body" and the diagram label "normally no body" say.

Live probe separates the two 404s: GET /api/v1/orders/99999999999 and /orders/abc both answer 404 with Content-Length: 0 (no route matched, no action ran), while /orders/2147483647 and /orders/999999 answer 404 with application/problem+json from NotFound() inside Get — so the constraint rejects out-of-32-bit-range segments, not only non-numeric ones. refs/aspnetcore-docs routing.md constraint table: `int` | `{id:int}` | `123456789`, `-123456789` | "Matches any integer". refs/dotnet-docs: `int` = "-2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 | Signed 32-bit integer".

claim_verdicts.evidence: Claim added and verified in this same round-3 pass, using this reviewer's own already-gathered evidence: RFC 9110 9.3.4 requires 201 on PUT-creates and states no condition on id selection; the lesson's clause is a defensible inference from the client naming its own request target, not an RFC rule, which is exactly what the claim text says.

issues.text: Unlisted claim: the condition attached to PUT-as-create. Claim 1 covers only "a successful PUT that creates a resource MUST answer 201"; nothing in .meta.json covers the added restriction "only where the client itself picks the id". RFC 9110 9.3.4 states no such condition — it follows from the client naming the request target, not from a rule in the spec. The sentence is defensible as written (a client that PUTs to a URL has by definition chosen that URL), but a bare "only" with no ledger entry is the kind of hidden assumption the ledger exists to record.
issues.quote: but only where the client itself picks the id it puts in the URL, instead of the server picking one as with `POST`
issues.fix: Leave the lesson text alone and add claim 10 to .meta.json: {"n":10,"section":4,"kind":"behavior","version_key":"http","text":"RFC 9110 9.3.4 requires 201 when a PUT creates the resource and sets no condition on who chooses the id; the lesson's 'only where the client itself picks the id' follows from the client naming the request target, not from a rule in the RFC.","source_hint":"RFC 9110 Section 9.3.4","needs_verification":false}.
